Part 1 · Layers of protection

Why is protection built in layers, and what makes a layer count?

Part 1 · the plan

From one safeguard to an onion of them

  1. Why layersfailures of equipment and people, often more than one at a time
  2. The onionprocess design inside, emergency response outside; which layers need power
  3. Control, alarms and the SISwhat each instrumented layer does and how it acts
  4. Relief, containment, responsethe outer layers that need no computer
  5. Independencethe property that lets a layer be counted at all

1 · Why layers

Three demands on any protection scheme

Cover many failures

Equipment, control and people fail, often together.

Respond in proportion

Stop only what must stop; keep producing.

Keep reserves

A worse event meets a stronger, outer layer.

Hazards here: SO₂ and SO₃ gas, acid, molten sulfur, steam, hot catalyst.

2 · The onion · click a layer, then cut the power

Seven rings between the hazard and people

automatic?
needs power?
needs a person?
layers still standing

Power loss takes BPCS and alarms together, yet the SIS still acts by de-energising — relief, containment and response need no power at all.

3 · Control, alarms and the SIS

Layers 1 and 2: control, then a personstep 1 of 2

1 · BPCS

Controls unstable and quick variables; slow ones (fouling, catalyst ageing) are only monitored. Each valve fails to its safest position.

2 · Alarms

No automatic action: a person decides. Priorities High, Medium, Low; a 1 % deadband stops repeats.

3 · Control, alarms and the SIS

Layer 3: the safety instrumented systemstep 2 of 2

Discrete and strong

Automatic action: stops part of the plant (here, the sulfur).

No automatic restart

Manual reset, then the start permissives.

Independent

Own sensor, own logic solver, own final element.

De-energise to trip

Lost power or air gives the safe state.

4 · Relief · move the vessel pressure

Layer 4: a valve the process opens itself

Layers 1–3 need power and a computer. Relief needs neither: process pressure lifts it.

relief valve

MAWP = maximum allowable working pressure of the vessel (API 521 ladder).

Set at or below 100 %, fully open by 110 %, reseat near 93 % — normal operation stays at or below 90 % so the valve stays shut.

4 · Relief, containment, response

Layers 5 and 6: when material is already out

5 · Containment

Passive or remote: bunds, kerbs, drains, isolation valves, stack height.

6 · Emergency response

Evacuation, fire fighting, health care. Needs a written plan, drills and community links.

Both depend on people under stress; their equipment is tested least often.

5 · Independence

A layer counts only if one failure cannot also defeat it

Own sensor, own logic, own final element.

A shared element is a common cause: one failure removes two layers.

Part 1 · summary

What part 1 settled

  • Protection is an onion: process design, BPCS, alarms, SIS, relief, containment, emergency response.
  • BPCS, alarms and SIS all need power; the SIS fails safe by de-energising.
  • Relief is self-actuating: normal operation stays at or below 90 % of MAWP.
  • A layer counts only with its own sensor, logic and final element.

4 · The SIS

Six trips, one logic solver, one shut-off valve

The second shut-off (FV-103) is a command through the DCS, not an SIS output.

5 · The outer layers

Relief, containment, response: mostly to be added

4 · Relief 5 rec.

Steam-side PSVs; thermal relief on BFW and acid; R-201 rated for blower shut-off (assumed).

5 · Containment 7 of 8

Acid bund to neutralisation pit, EIVs, sulfur pit, snuffing; stack exists.

6 · Response 11 rec.

SO₂ detectors, windsocks, muster points, SCBA, showers, hydrants.

Part 2 · summary

What part 2 settled

  • The register holds 104 items: 46 BPCS, 22 alarm, 12 SIS, 5 relief, 8 containment, 11 response.
  • Every valve fails to its safe side: sulfur shut, air open, TV-201 closed.
  • Each trip has a pre-alarm in front of it; six trips all close XV-103.
  • Relief, containment and response are almost all recommended additions.

Part 3 · Operating windows and independence

How far is each variable from damage, and can one failure defeat two layers?

Part 3 · the plan

Limits in a row, layers kept apart

  1. The operating windowtarget, alarm, SIS and critical limits, each leaving time for the next layer
  2. Seven windows of this unitmove a value outward and see which layer acts
  3. Stack SO₂ on a log scale292 ppm to 5000 ppm spans more than a decade
  4. Independence tracewhich control, alarm and trip each element feeds
  5. Gaps and fixesTE-203B, FT-301B and XY-103B

1 · The operating window

Four limits, each a hand-over to the next layer

The register lists the layers. Do their limits leave each layer time to act?

An integrity operating window (IOW) places the limits in order.

Each gap must give the next layer time: the alarm early enough for a person, the trip before damage.

2 · Seven windows · pick a variable, move its value

Which layer acts at this value?

layer acting

Acid strength and gas to the IPA have no trip — there the alarm and the operator are the last instrumented layer.

Part 3 · summary

What part 3 settled

  • Each variable has a window: target, alarm, trip, critical limit.
  • Stack SO₂ needs a log scale: 292 ppm design, 500 permit, 3000 trip.
  • TE-203, FT-301 and XV-103 each serve more than one layer.
  • Fixes: TE-203B, FT-301B and XY-103B.

This deck

Key Takeaways

1

Count a layer only if it is independent of the cause and of the others.

2

Remember BPCS, alarms and SIS share power; relief and containment do not.

3

Read every variable as a window: target, alarm, trip, damage.

4

Keep a pre-alarm in front of every trip, with time for a person to act.

5

Give each trip its own sensor and a second final element.
